input: It is important to note that vapour-compression refrigeration plays a crucial role in modern cold storage, and the performance of such a system can be meaningfully evaluated by comparing its actual behaviour against the theoretical Carnot limit. In the case considered here, a vapour-compression unit serves a cold store, evaporating at −25 °C and condensing at 35 °C. When these temperatures are converted to absolute terms, the evaporating temperature is 248.15 K and the condensing temperature is 308.15 K, giving an overall temperature lift of 60 K. The Carnot coefficient of performance (COP) between these two temperatures is obtained by dividing the evaporating temperature by the lift, 248.15/60, which yields a value of 4.13. This value represents an idealised upper bound that no real machine operating between the same temperatures can exceed, underscoring the gap that inevitably separates practical equipment from the reversible ideal. The cycle itself proceeds through compression, condensation, throttling, and evaporation, and irreversibilities are distributed across each of these steps in ways that are difficult to isolate individually. In practice, the installed unit achieves a COP of 1.84, which corresponds to approximately 0.45 of the Carnot value. The difference between 1.84 and 4.13 can be attributed to a range of losses associated with the compressor, the throttling process, and the heat exchangers, each of which contributes to the overall shortfall in its own way. It should also be emphasised that the achieved figure comes from the manufacturer's test conducted at full load, and part-load performance is not stated, meaning that the behaviour of the unit under the varying conditions typically encountered in day-to-day operation remains somewhat uncertain. Overall, the comparison highlights that, between −25 °C and 35 °C, no refrigerator can exceed a COP of 4.13, while the tested unit reaches 1.84 at full load, highlighting the importance of interpreting test figures with appropriate care.
target: A vapour-compression unit serves the cold store, evaporating at −25 °C and condensing at 35 °C. The coefficient of performance (COP) of a refrigerator is the heat removed from the cold space divided by the work supplied. In kelvin, the evaporating temperature is 248.15 K and the condensing temperature is 308.15 K, a lift of 60 K. The Carnot COP between the two temperatures is the evaporating temperature divided by the lift, 248.15/60, and comes to 4.13. No refrigerator working between the same two temperatures can pass that value, because the Carnot cycle is reversible and every real cycle carries losses the reversible cycle does not. The unit runs four steps in a loop: the compressor raises the vapour pressure, the condenser rejects heat and condenses the vapour, the throttling valve drops the pressure, and the evaporator takes up heat from the store as the liquid boils. The installed unit achieves a COP of 1.84, which is 0.45 of the Carnot value. The distance between 1.84 and 4.13 is the sum of the losses in the compressor, the throttling valve, and the heat exchangers. Compression falls short of the isentropic ideal, the valve throws away the expansion work an expander would return, and each exchanger needs a temperature difference of its own to pass heat at all. The achieved figure is from the manufacturer's test at full load. Part-load performance is not stated, and the test gives no COP for the part-load conditions under which a cold store runs for much of the year. An annual energy estimate for the store built on the full-load figure carries the full-load condition with it. Between −25 °C and 35 °C, the Carnot limit is a COP of 4.13, and the tested unit reaches 1.84 at the single condition at which it was measured.
